text: A general plan or master plan for a metropolitan area is in effect a policy statement as to how that area should be spatially arranged. Such plans clearly show that decentralization of population/commerce/industry is continuously progressing outwardly from the city. In the process, large open spaces are often skipped. The zoning or location of commerce/industry many miles away from the city in no way means there is lack of economic/social/political interface of the commerce or industry with the base city. A metropolitan area is a series of overlapping markets of donut or irregular shapes which separately and together compete to attract commerce/industry and to serve consumers. Modern transportation networks and communication systems tie the numerous communities within a metropolitan area together and offset much of the effect of distance. Many industries locate on outer fringes because of zoning, land requirements, environmental restrictions, or the need for speedy access to a circumferential/ radial highway system permitting fast travel into, away from, and throughout the metropolitan area to its various sectors. These industries are dependent upon many resources of the metropolitan area which may include labor, management. materials, supplies, food, utilities, financial services, transportation, market channels, and others. If the resources needed--including the transportation network--are not available within a developed area, the industries will not locate there. The fact that there are few industries in outlying areas occupying small percentages of total land does not obviate the strength of economic, social/ political links of those industries with the rest of the metropolitan area. Richmond, Virginia was used in the previously referenced representation of the Short Haul Survival Committee to illustrate the questionnaire their consultant used for eighteen cities. Richmond is a prime example of a city with fast-developing peripheral areas.
